rv.q: Two London theatres offer just the right shows, both beguiling and, in both, wily women use their wit and words to outrun the plans of a tyrannical man. To Shakespeare’s Forest of Arden first, where Rosalind and Celia turn banishment from court into a form of liberation, in a gorgeous staging of As You Like It at the Soho Place theatre.

The lovers, outcasts and locals who wander through Arden tip winks to its composer pianist, Michael Bruce, and will him to “shut up” or to play on cue. That mime is part of a grander concept behind director Josie Rourke’s delicate and delightful production, which finds a perfect balance between West End spectacle and Shakespearean purity.

A pianist is on stage throughout, playing jaunty incidental music and songs that lift the show. There are period costumes and an air of dreamy fantasy as the “country copulatives” work through their love tangles. Alfred Enoch and Leah Harvey are lovely as Orlando and Rosalind, but Rourke won’t let the play’s magic talk for itself.

Ayling-Ellis’s Celia, Alfred Enoch’s distracted nerd Orlando, Leah Harvey’s chipper urchin Rosalind and big-ish name US actor Martha Plimpton’s uncomfortably over-emotional Jacques are all good fun, but feel like they’re virtually in different plays.

The finest moment comes from Martha Plimpton, who is a magnificent Jaques. Looking as if she might have strolled over from a Restoration coffee shop – big hair, breeches, long clay pipe – she irradiates the seven ages of man speech, so that it too is a celebration of fluidity and variety.

At its best, the staging has a golden-russet shimmer, as if it’s aglow with dreamy passions. At its worst, it’s over-emphatic and laborious, and, as a romantic comedy, it’s significantly stronger on the rom than the com. But Rourke draws some touching performances from her cast, with Leah Harvey an entrancing and intelligent Rosalind.

And the picturesque accessibility of the production affirms that, with its gentle mirth and breezy melancholy (languidly incarnated by Plimpton’s Jacques), the play offers a restorative counter to end­-of-year gloom.
